content: For zinc, two systematic reviews were conducted to assess the impact of fortifying staple foods on health-related outcomes and biomarkers of zinc status in the general population. For vitamin A, one systematic review evaluated the effects of fortifying staple foods on vitamin A deficiency and associated health outcomes in the general population. The evidence from these systematic reviews was utilized to develop the evidence-to-decision framework and draft the guideline. GRADE summary of findings tables for each critical outcome were prepared based on commissioned (Cochrane) systematic reviews. For iron, a systematic review was commissioned to evaluate the benefits and harms of fortifying wheat flour with iron alone or in combination with other vitamins and minerals on anemia, iron status, and health-related outcomes. This review included cluster and individual randomized controlled trials conducted in general populations aged two years and older across various countries. Ten trials involving 3,319 participants were included, with intervention durations ranging from 3 to 24 months. Compared to unfortified flour, wheat flour fortified with iron alone or with other micronutrients may reduce anemia and likely has little or no effect on iron deficiency. The effect of iron-fortified wheat flour on increasing hemoglobin concentrations remains uncertain. A group of six systematic reviews on food fortification, including wheat flour fortified with iron and other micronutrients, was also reviewed. Studies across all socioeconomic strata demonstrated that flour fortification with iron is an effective strategy to improve iron status in populations, including large-scale food fortification programs in lowand middle-income countries. Government-supported fortification programs targeting children and women of reproductive age showed statistically significant reductions in anemia prevalence and low serum/plasma ferritin concentrations. Randomized controlled trials on iron-fortified foods, including wheat flour products like bread, snacks, noodles, and biscuits, in children under 10 years of age showed a significant increase in hemoglobin concentrations in the fortified group compared to controls. A systematic review of studies on staple food fortification in women of reproductive age and pregnant women reported significant increases in serum ferritin and hemoglobin levels. Another systematic review of 60 randomized and pseudo-randomized controlled trials found that consumption of iron-fortified or biofortified foods significantly improved hemoglobin, serum ferritin, and iron status while reducing the risk of anemia and iron deficiency. For folic acid, a systematic review was commissioned to evaluate the effects of fortifying wheat and maize flour with folic acid on population health outcomes. Seven studies involving fortified wheat flour were included. The authors concluded that folic acid, alone or with other micronutrients, may increase erythrocyte and serum/plasma folate concentrations. For zinc, a systematic review assessed the beneficial and adverse effects of fortifying staple foods with zinc on health-related outcomes and biomarkers of zinc status in the general population. Eight trials with 709 participants were included, five of which focused on wheat flour or wheat products. The authors concluded that zinc fortification may improve serum zinc status if zinc is the sole micronutrient used for fortification. However, when zinc is added in combination with other micronutrients, it may have little or no effect on serum zinc concentrations. There was no statistical difference in the effect on plasma zinc concentration or zinc deficiency by food vehicle group (e.g., cereal grains, beverages, condiments). Studies focusing solely on wheat flour/products showed no effect of zinc fortification on the prevalence of zinc deficiency. For vitamin A, a systematic review evaluated the effects of fortifying staple foods with vitamin A to reduce vitamin A deficiency and improve health-related outcomes in the general population older than two years. The review included interventions fortifying staple foods with vitamin A alone or in combination with other vitamins and minerals. Only two studies reported on wheat flour as the intervention vehicle for fortification, with intervention durations ranging from 3 to 9 months. The WHO guideline development group considered critical outcomes for decision-making, including iron status, iron deficiency, anemia, neural tube defects, congenital anomalies, folate status, zinc deficiency, zinc status, and growth (e.g., stunting, wasting, underweight). Adverse effects were considered for all micronutrients. Using the GRADE methodology, the certainty of direct evidence for critical outcomes was rated as low or very low. The overarching principle of the recommendations is that fortification of cereal flours, particularly industrially processed wheat flour, should be considered when flour is regularly consumed by large population groups in a country. The fortification scheme, including which nutrients to add and in what amounts, should be based on the nutritional needs of the population, usual consumption of fortifiable flour, sensory and physical effects of added nutrients, type of wheat and flour extraction rate, other fortified food items or ongoing micronutrient programs, and fortification costs, feasibility, and acceptance. The recommendations for wheat flour fortification are as follows: Fortification with highly bioavailable iron is recommended as a public health strategy to improve hemoglobin concentrations and iron status and to prevent anemia and iron deficiency, particularly in vulnerable groups such as children and women (strong recommendation, low certainty of evidence). Fortification with folic acid is recommended as a public health strategy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects in pregnancies among women of reproductive age and to improve folate status in populations (strong recommendation, low and very low certainty of evidence). Fortification with zinc may be used as a public health strategy to improve serum/plasma zinc status in populations (conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). The guideline development group considered wheat flour fortification with iron and folic acid as strong recommendations despite the low certainty of evidence, based on the priority of the problem and the clear benefits of fortification. Other considerations included feasibility and acceptability of the intervention. Remarks for implementation include: In settings where vitamin A deficiency is a public health problem and other strategies are insufficient, wheat flour fortification with vitamin A could be considered to improve vitamin A status or reduce subclinical vitamin A deficiency. In countries with high prevalence of vitamin B12 deficiency, inclusion of vitamin B12 in staple food fortification with folic acid could prevent imbalances caused by folic acid alone. Restoration of thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and pyridoxine in refined wheat flour could be considered as a regular practice in fortification. The choice of iron compound should balance cost, bioavailability, micronutrient interactions, and acceptance of sensory attributes like texture, taste, smell, and color. Removal of phytates in wheat flour could enhance the bioavailability of iron and zinc. Addition of vitamins and minerals should be based on evidence of micronutrient inadequacies or deficiencies, with pre-fortification data used to measure program impact. Countries fortifying wheat flour may also fortify other food items, with a combined strategy using multiple vehicles to reach all population segments. Fortification programs should be integrated and monitored as part of national efforts to prevent and control micronutrient deficiencies. Food fortification should adhere to national standards with quality assurance and control systems to ensure high-quality implementation. Monitoring consumption patterns and evaluating micronutrient status can inform adjustments to fortification levels over time. Populations should be encouraged to achieve adequate nutrition through a healthy, balanced diet, with fortified foods serving as a complement when necessary. Although evidence is limited, wheat flour fortification could potentially reduce inequities in access to and consumption of essential micronutrients, improving health outcomes and preventing adverse effects.
